concepts: Trigonometric equations: range of a parameter for which a solution exists
questions.question: The set of all values of $\lambda$ for which the equation $\cos^2 2x-2\sin^4 x-2\cos^2 x=\lambda$ has a real solution $x$, is :
questions.key_idea: Write $\lambda$ as a polynomial in $\cos^2x\in[0,1]$; the set of $\lambda$ is the range of that quadratic.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\cos 2x=c$ as the single variable: $\sin^2x=\frac{1-c}2$ and $\cos^2x=\frac{1+c}2$ remove the quartic completely.
solution: As $x$ varies, $c^2=\cos^22x$ takes every value in $[0,1]$.
Hence $\lambda$ takes every value from $\frac{0-3}{2}=-\frac32$ to $\frac{1-3}{2}=-1$: $\left[-\frac32,-1\right]$, option (D). Same answer.

useful_results: $\sin^2x=\frac{1-\cos2x}{2}$ and $\cos^2x=\frac{1+\cos2x}{2}$: any even-degree expression in $\sin x,\cos x$ becomes a polynomial in $\cos2x\in[-1,1]$.
Here $\cos^22x-2\sin^4x-2\cos^2x=\frac{\cos^22x-3}{2}$ exactly (checked: $x=0$ gives $-1$, $x=\frac\pi4$ gives $-\frac32$).
Range of $p(u)=\alpha u^2+\beta u+\gamma$ on $[m,M]$: compare the end values with the vertex value $p\left(-\frac{\beta}{2\alpha}\right)$ only if the vertex lies inside $[m,M]$.
\"Equation $f(x)=\lambda$ has a real solution\" means exactly that $\lambda$ lies in the range of $f$.

questions.question: If the solution of the equation $\log_{\cos x}\cot x+4\log_{\sin x}\tan x=1$, $x\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$, is $\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\alpha+\sqrt\beta}{2}\right)$ where $\alpha,\beta$ are integers, then $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: After the base change the equation is homogeneous in $\log\sin x,\log\cos x$ and collapses to $\log\sin x=2\log\cos x$.
solution: Change of base: $\frac{\log\cos x-\log\sin x}{\log\cos x}+4\cdot\frac{\log\sin x-\log\cos x}{\log\sin x}=1$.
Multiply by $\log\sin x\log\cos x$ and simplify: $(\log\sin x)^2-4(\log\sin x)(\log\cos x)+4(\log\cos x)^2=0$ (the PDF writes $=1$ here; it must be $0$).
This is $(\log\sin x-2\log\cos x)^2=0$, so $\log\sin x=2\log\cos x$.
questions.correction_note: PDF step 3 ends with '= 1' ((log sin x)^2 - 4 (log sin x)(log cos x) + 4 (log cos x)^2 = 1'). Multiplying the equation by log sin x log cos x and cancelling the common ab term gives '= 0'; with '= 1' the next line (log sin x = 2 log cos x) would not follow. Corrected to 0; the final answer 4 is unchanged. The PDF also does not say that the negative root of sin x is rejected on (0, pi/2); added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Let $p=\log_{\cos x}\sin x$; then $\log_{\sin x}\cos x=\frac1p$ and the equation becomes $p+\frac4p=4$, solved by AM-GM.
solution: On $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$ both $\sin x,\cos x\in(0,1)$, so both logarithms are negative and $p=\log_{\cos x}\sin x=\frac{\log\sin x}{\log\cos x}>0$.
$\log_{\cos x}\cot x=\log_{\cos x}\cos x-\log_{\cos x}\sin x=1-p$.
$\log_{\sin x}\tan x=\log_{\sin x}\sin x-\log_{\sin x}\cos x=1-\frac1p$.
For $p>0$, AM-GM gives $p+\frac4p\ge2\sqrt4=4$, with equality only when $p=\frac4p$, i.e. $p=2$.
So $\log\sin x=2\log\cos x$, $\sin x=\cos^2x$, $\sin x=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}$, giving $\alpha=-1,\beta=5$ and $\alpha+\beta=4$. Same answer.

useful_results: $\log_ab\cdot\log_ba=1$ and $\log_a\frac bc=\log_ab-\log_ac$: reducing everything to $p=\log_ab$ turns a log equation into $p+\frac kp=m$.
For $p>0$: $p+\frac kp\ge2\sqrt k$ with equality iff $p=\sqrt k$ - a perfect-square equation $p+\frac4p=4$ has the single root $p=2$.
A homogeneous quadratic $a^2-4ab+4b^2=0$ in two logs is $(a-2b)^2=0$: spot the perfect square before using the formula.

Domain: the bases $\cos x,\sin x$ must be positive and different from $1$ and $\cot x,\tan x$ positive; $x\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$ guarantees this (and $\sin x=\frac{\sqrt5-1}2$ is neither $0$ nor $1$).
$\sin x=\cos^2x$ gives $\sin x=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}\approx0.618$, the reciprocal of the golden ratio (check: $0.618^2+0.618-1\approx0$).

questions.question: Let $S=\{\theta\in[0,2\pi):\tan(\pi\cos\theta)+\tan(\pi\sin\theta)=0\}$. Then $\sum_{\theta\in S}\sin^2\left(\theta+\frac\pi4\right)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $\tan A=-\tan B$ forces $\pi\cos\theta+\pi\sin\theta=n\pi$, and $|\sin\theta+\cos\theta|\le\sqrt2$ leaves only $n=-1,0,1$.
solution: (Check: at each of these six angles $\cos\theta,\sin\theta$ are not half-odd integers, so both tangents are defined.)
$\sin^2\left(\theta+\frac\pi4\right)=\frac{(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^2}{2}=\frac{n^2}{2}$: it equals $\frac12$ for the four angles with $n=\pm1$ and $0$ for the two with $n=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Combine the tangents: $\tan A+\tan B=\frac{\sin(A+B)}{\cos A\cos B}$, and work with $\varphi=\theta+\frac\pi4$ so that the required sum never needs the individual $\theta$.
solution: $\tan A+\tan B=\frac{\sin(A+B)}{\cos A\cos B}=0\iff\sin(A+B)=0$ (with $\cos A\cos B\ne0$).

$\sin\varphi=\pm\frac1{\sqrt2}$ has $2$ solutions each in $\left[\frac\pi4,\frac{9\pi}4\right)$ (namely $\frac\pi4,\frac{3\pi}4$ and $\frac{5\pi}4,\frac{7\pi}4$): $4$ angles, each contributing $\sin^2\varphi=\frac12$.

useful_results: $\tan A=\tan B\iff A=B+n\pi$; $\tan A+\tan B=0\iff\sin(A+B)=0$ (when $\cos A\cos B\ne0$) $\iff A+B=n\pi$.
$a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\sin(\theta+\varphi)$, so $\sin\theta+\cos\theta=n$ has solutions only for integer $|n|\le\sqrt2$, i.e. $n\in\{-1,0,1\}$.
$\sin^2\left(\theta+\frac\pi4\right)=\frac{1+\sin2\theta}{2}=\frac{(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^2}{2}$: sums over solutions of $\sin\theta+\cos\theta=n$ need only $n^2$.
Always check the domain: $\tan(\pi\cos\theta)$ is undefined when $\cos\theta=\pm\frac12,\pm\frac32,\dots$; none of the six solutions hits this.

concepts: Trigonometric equations: product-to-sum and general solution of $\cos A=\cos B$
questions.question: If $m$ and $n$ respectively are the numbers of positive and negative values of $\theta$ in the interval $[-\pi,\pi]$ that satisfy the equation $\cos2\theta\cos\frac\theta2=\cos3\theta\cos\frac{9\theta}2$, then $mn$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: After product-to-sum the $\cos\frac{3\theta}2$ terms cancel, leaving $\cos\frac{15\theta}2=\cos\frac{5\theta}2$.
solution: Multiply by $2$ and use $2\cos A\cos B=\cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B)$ on both sides.
$\cos\frac{5\theta}2+\cos\frac{3\theta}2=\cos\frac{15\theta}2+\cos\frac{3\theta}2$ (the PDF prints the last term as $\cos\frac{3\theta}{1}$, a typo for $\cos\frac{3\theta}2$).
The family $\theta=\frac{2n\pi}5$ is contained in $\theta=\frac{n\pi}5$, so all solutions are $\theta=\frac{p\pi}5$, $p\in I$.
Positive values: $p=1,\dots,5$, so $m=5$; negative values: $p=-1,\dots,-5$, so $n=5$ ($p=0$ is neither).
questions.correction_note: Typo in the PDF's second line: it prints 'cos 3theta/1' where cos(3theta/2) is meant (3theta + 9theta/2 and 9theta/2 - 3theta give 15theta/2 and 3theta/2). The working that follows is correct and the answer 25 is unchanged. I also added the line that the family 2n pi/5 lies inside n pi/5 and that theta=0 is neither positive nor negative.

alternate_solutions.idea: Subtract instead of equate: $\cos X-\cos Y=-2\sin\frac{X+Y}2\sin\frac{X-Y}2$ gives a product of sines, and one factor's zeros contain the other's.
solution: Now $\sin5\theta=2\sin\frac{5\theta}2\cos\frac{5\theta}2$, so every zero of $\sin\frac{5\theta}2$ is a zero of $\sin5\theta$.
Therefore the equation is equivalent to $\sin5\theta=0$, i.e. $\theta=\frac{k\pi}5$.
The solution set is symmetric about $0$ because the original equation is even in $\theta$; $k=-5,\dots,5$ gives $11$ solutions, one of them $\theta=0$.

useful_results: $2\cos A\cos B=\cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B)$; $\cos X=\cos Y\iff X=2n\pi\pm Y$; $\cos X-\cos Y=-2\sin\frac{X+Y}2\sin\frac{X-Y}2$.
When two solution families are written as $\frac{2n\pi}5$ and $\frac{n\pi}5$, take their union: here the first is a subset of the second, so nothing is double counted.
If the equation is unchanged by $\theta\to-\theta$ (both sides are even), then positive and negative solutions are equal in number, so $m=n$ and $mn=m^2$.
Number of multiples of $\frac\pi k$ in $[-\pi,\pi]$ is $2k+1$ (here $11$); remove $\theta=0$ before counting positives and negatives.

questions.question: Let $S=\left\{x\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right):9^{1-\tan^2x}+9^{\tan^2x}=10\right\}$ and $\beta=\sum_{x\in S}\tan^2\left(\frac x3\right)$, then $\frac16(\beta-14)^2$ is equal to :

alternate_solutions.idea: The function $9^t+9^{1-t}$ is convex and symmetric about $t=\frac12$, so the roots of $=10$ can be spotted ($t=0,1$) and there are no others.
solution: $f$ is convex ($f''>0$), so $f(t)=10$ has at most two roots; hence $t=0,1$ are all.

useful_results: $a^t+a^{c-t}$ is symmetric about $t=\frac c2$ and convex for $a>1$: an equation $a^t+a^{c-t}=k$ has at most two roots, $t$ and $c-t$.
Equations of type $y+\frac k y=m$ with $y=a^{t}$: $y^2-my+k=0$; here $y=1,9$.
$\tan^2\frac\theta2=\frac{1-\cos\theta}{1+\cos\theta}$; $\tan\frac\pi{12}=2-\sqrt3$, $\tan\frac{5\pi}{12}=2+\sqrt3$.
For an even function summed over a solution set symmetric about $0$, add twice the positive part: here the $x=\pm\frac\pi4$ terms are equal.

concepts: Trigonometric equations: factorisation and number of solutions in $[0,2\pi]$
questions.question: The number of elements in the set $S=\left\{\theta\in[0,2\pi]:3\cos^4\theta-5\cos^2\theta-2\sin^6\theta+2=0\right\}$ is :
questions.key_idea: Split $-5\cos^2\theta+2=-3\cos^2\theta+2\sin^2\theta$ so the expression factors as $\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta(2\sin^2\theta-1)$.
solution: $3\cos^2\theta(\cos^2\theta-1)+2\sin^2\theta(1-\sin^4\theta)=0$ (the PDF has $\sin^4\theta-1$ with the wrong sign).
questions.correction_note: PDF line 4: '3cos^2(cos^2-1) + 2 sin^2 (sin^4 - 1)'. Since 2 sin^2 - 2 sin^6 = 2 sin^2 (1 - sin^4), the sign inside the bracket should be (1 - sin^4), and the PDF's next line (with a stray '-1') is garbled. The final factorisation sin^2 cos^2 (2 sin^2 - 1) = 0 and the answer 9 are correct; rewritten the two lines minimally.

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $w=\cos2\theta$: the whole expression becomes $\frac{w(w^2-1)}4$, so the equation says $\cos2\theta\in\{0,1,-1\}$ - count by $2\theta\in[0,4\pi]$.
solution: Let $u=\cos^2\theta$, so $\sin^2\theta=1-u$ and the expression is $3u^2-5u-2(1-u)^3+2=2u^3-3u^2+u=u(2u-1)(u-1)$.
Total $4+3+2=9$ distinct values of $\theta$. Same answer.

useful_results: For an expression in $\sin^2\theta,\cos^2\theta$, set $u=\cos^2\theta$ (or $w=\cos2\theta$) and factor the resulting polynomial; the equation here becomes $u(2u-1)(u-1)=0$.
$\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta(2\sin^2\theta-1)=-\frac{\sin^22\theta\cos2\theta}{4}$: all three factors give $\cos2\theta\in\{0,\pm1\}$ at once.
On the closed interval $[0,2\pi]$ count both ends: $\sin\theta=0$ has $3$ roots, $\cos\theta=0$ has $2$, $\cos2\theta=0$ has $4$, $\cos2\theta=1$ has $3$, $\cos2\theta=-1$ has $2$.
Useful expansions: $\sin^4+\cos^4=1-2\sin^2\cos^2$ and $\sin^6+\cos^6=1-3\sin^2\cos^2$.

concepts: Trigonometric equations: number of solutions in an interval
questions.question: If $2\tan^2\theta-5\sec\theta=1$ has exactly $7$ solutions in the interval $\left[0,\frac{n\pi}2\right]$, for the least value of $n\in N$, then $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac k{2^k}$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Solutions of $\cos\theta=\frac13$ come as $\alpha,2\pi-\alpha,2\pi+\alpha,\dots$; the seventh is $6\pi+\alpha$, which fixes $n=13$.
solution: With $\alpha=\cos^{-1}\frac13\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$ the solutions in increasing order are $\alpha,\,2\pi-\alpha,\,2\pi+\alpha,\,4\pi-\alpha,\,4\pi+\alpha,\,6\pi-\alpha,\,6\pi+\alpha$.
The seventh is $6\pi+\alpha<6\pi+\frac\pi2=\frac{13\pi}2$, so for exactly $7$ solutions the least $n$ is $13$ (for $n=12$ only $6$ solutions fit in $[0,6\pi]$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Telescope the sum: $\frac k{2^k}=a_{k-1}-a_k$ with $a_k=\frac{k+2}{2^k}$, so $\sum_{k=1}^nk2^{-k}=2-\frac{n+2}{2^n}$ without any subtraction trick.
solution: The count of solutions is unchanged: the $7$th root of $\cos\theta=\frac13$ is $6\pi+\alpha$, so $n=13$.

useful_results: $\sum_{k=1}^nk\,r^{k}$ for $r=\frac12$: $\sum_{k=1}^n\frac k{2^k}=2-\frac{n+2}{2^n}$ (checked: $n=13$ gives $1.99817$; direct sum $1.99817$); it tends to $2$.
For $0<c<1$, the positive solutions of $\cos\theta=c$ are $\alpha,\,2\pi-\alpha,\,2\pi+\alpha,\,4\pi-\alpha,\dots$: the $(2j+1)$-th is $2j\pi+\alpha$, the $2j$-th is $2j\pi-\alpha$.
$\sec\theta$ and $\csc\theta$ never lie in $(-1,1)$, so $\sec\theta=-\frac12$ gives no solution - reject such roots immediately.
Reduce $\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta-1$ to get a quadratic in $\sec\theta$ (or $\cos\theta$) before solving.

questions.question: If $\alpha,-\frac\pi2<\alpha<\frac\pi2$ is the solution of $4\cos\theta+5\sin\theta=1$, then the value of $\tan\alpha$ is :
questions.key_idea: Divide by $\cos\theta$ and square: $(4+5\tan\theta)^2=1+\tan^2\theta$ is a quadratic in $\tan\theta$; reject the root with $4+5\tan\theta<0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Geometry: $(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ is the intersection of the unit circle with the line $4x+5y=1$; find it with the foot of the perpendicular and read off $\frac yx$ for the point with $x>0$.
solution: The line $4x+5y=1$ has normal $(4,5)$; its foot from the origin is $\frac{(4,5)}{41}$, at distance $\frac1{\sqrt{41}}$.
Half-chord length on the unit circle: $\sqrt{1-\frac1{41}}=\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{\sqrt{41}}$, in the direction $\frac{(-5,4)}{\sqrt{41}}$.
Numerically $-0.5698$; direct check $4\cos\alpha+5\sin\alpha=1$. Same answer, option (D).

useful_results: For $a\cos\theta+b\sin\theta=c$ the squared-tangent form is $(b^2-c^2)T^2+2abT+(a^2-c^2)=0$ with $T=\tan\theta$ (here $24T^2+40T+15=0$); solutions exist iff $|c|\le\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.
Squaring creates an extraneous root. Test each root with the sign condition that was lost: here $\sec\theta>0\Rightarrow4+5T>0$.
Both roots of the quadratic correspond to the two solutions of the equation in $[0,2\pi)$; the interval restriction $\cos\alpha>0$ picks one.
The two solutions are the endpoints of a chord of the unit circle cut by the line $ax+by=c$, symmetric about the direction $(a,b)$.
Check: product of the roots $\frac{a^2-c^2}{b^2-c^2}=\frac{15}{24}=0.625$ equals $(-0.5698)(-1.0969)$.

questions.question: The sum of the solutions $x\in R$ of the equation $\frac{3\cos2x+\cos^32x}{\cos^6x-\sin^6x}=x^3-x^2+6$ is :
questions.key_idea: $\cos^6x-\sin^6x=\cos2x\left(1-\sin^2x\cos^2x\right)$ makes the left side collapse to the constant $4$.
solution: Also $4-\sin^22x=3+\cos^22x$, so the fraction is $1$ and LHS $=4$ (valid when $\cos2x\ne0$).
The only real root is $x=-1$ (and $\cos(-2)\ne0$), so the sum of the real solutions is $-1$: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $c=\cos2x$ and $\cos^2x=\frac{1+c}2$, $\sin^2x=\frac{1-c}2$: then $\cos^6x-\sin^6x=\frac{3c+c^3}4$ - exactly a quarter of the numerator.
solution: $f'(x)=3x^2-2x$ vanishes at $x=0$ (local max, $f(0)=2>0$) and $x=\frac23$ (local min, $f\left(\frac23\right)=\frac{50}{27}>0$), so $f$ has exactly one real root.
$f(-1)=0$, hence the real root is $x=-1$ and the sum is $-1$, option (C). Same answer.

useful_results: $\cos^6x-\sin^6x=\frac{\cos2x\left(3+\cos^22x\right)}4$; in general $\cos^2x=\frac{1+\cos2x}2$, $\sin^2x=\frac{1-\cos2x}2$ turns powers into polynomials in $\cos2x$.
Related: $\sin^4x+\cos^4x=\frac{3+\cos4x}4$ and $\sin^6x+\cos^6x=\frac{5+3\cos4x}8=1-\frac34\sin^22x$.
If one side of a 'transcendental' equation is secretly constant, the equation is a disguised polynomial; always keep the excluded points (here $\cos2x=0$) in mind.
Sum of real roots: only apply Vieta to the real roots. $x^3-x^2+2$ has roots $-1,\,1\pm i$, so the real sum is $-1$, not the Vieta sum $1$ - which is exactly the trap behind the printed key.
A cubic with local max and local min of the same sign has exactly one real root.

concepts: Trigonometric equations: number of solutions in an interval
Quadratic equations: nature and sign of roots
questions.question: If $2\sin^3x+\sin2x\cos x+4\sin x-4=0$ has exactly $3$ solutions in the interval $\left[0,\frac{n\pi}2\right]$, $n\in N$, then the roots of the equation $x^2+nx+(n-3)=0$ belongs to :
questions.key_idea: $\sin2x\cos x=2\sin x(1-\sin^2x)$ cancels the cubic term, leaving the linear equation $\sin x=\frac23$.
solution: Solutions of $\sin x=\frac23$ for $x\ge0$ are $\alpha,\ \pi-\alpha,\ 2\pi+\alpha,\ 3\pi-\alpha,\dots$ with $\alpha=\sin^{-1}\frac23\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$.
Exactly three solutions $\alpha,\pi-\alpha,2\pi+\alpha$ need $\frac{n\pi}2\ge2\pi+\alpha$ but $<3\pi-\alpha$; the graph shows this holds for $\frac{5\pi}2$, so $n=5$.
Roots $\alpha,\beta=\frac{-5\pm\sqrt{17}}2$; $\sqrt{17}<5$, so both are negative, i.e. they belong to $(-\infty,0)$: option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Group $2\sin^3x+2\sin x\cos^2x=2\sin x\left(\sin^2x+\cos^2x\right)=2\sin x$ at once, and read off the roots' signs from sum and product without solving the quadratic.
solution: $\sin2x\cos x=2\sin x\cos^2x$, so $2\sin^3x+\sin2x\cos x=2\sin x\left(\sin^2x+\cos^2x\right)=2\sin x$.
The equation is $2\sin x+4\sin x-4=0$, i.e. $\sin x=\frac23$.
On $[0,\infty)$ the solutions are $\alpha,\pi-\alpha,2\pi+\alpha,3\pi-\alpha,\dots$; exactly three need $2\pi+\alpha\le\frac{n\pi}2<3\pi-\alpha$.
Because $0<\alpha<\frac\pi2$, $n=5$ works: $\frac{5\pi}2=2\pi+\frac\pi2\ge2\pi+\alpha$ and $\frac{5\pi}2<3\pi-\alpha$; $n=4$ gives only two solutions and $n=6$ gives four.
Real roots with positive product and negative sum are both negative: $(-\infty,0)$, option (A). Same answer.

useful_results: Look for $\sin^2x+\cos^2x$ groupings first: $2\sin^3x+2\sin x\cos^2x=2\sin x$ (and similarly $\sin^3x\cos x+\sin x\cos^3x=\sin x\cos x$).

For $0<k<1$ the equation $\sin x=k$ has solutions in $[0,\infty)$ at $\alpha,\pi-\alpha,2\pi+\alpha,3\pi-\alpha,\dots$; exactly three solutions in $\left[0,\frac{n\pi}2\right]$ forces $n=5$ for every such $k$.
Signs of real roots of $x^2+px+q$ ($D>0$): both negative iff $p>0,q>0$; both positive iff $p<0,q>0$; opposite signs iff $q<0$.
Check: $x^2+5x+2$ has roots $\approx-0.438$ and $-4.562$.

questions.question: The number of solutions, of the equation $e^{\sin x}-2e^{-\sin x}=2$, is :
questions.key_idea: The substitution $y=e^{\sin x}$ gives $y=1+\sqrt3$, which would need $\sin x=\ln(1+\sqrt3)>1$.
solution: Let $y=e^{\sin x}$; since $e^{\sin x}>0$ for all $x$, $y>0$.
But $\sin x\le1$, so there is no solution: the number of solutions is $0$, option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Monotonicity: $g(s)=e^s-2e^{-s}$ is increasing, so its largest value for $s=\sin x\in[-1,1]$ is $g(1)=e-\frac2e<2$.
solution: Indeed $e-\frac2e<2\iff e^2-2e-2<0\iff e<1+\sqrt3$, which is true.
So the left side never reaches $2$: no solutions, answer $0$, option (A). Same answer.

useful_results: For $\sin x$ or $\cos x$ inside an exponential, put $y=e^{\sin x}\in\left[\frac1e,e\right]$ and test the roots of the algebraic equation against this window.
$g(s)=e^s-2e^{-s}$ is increasing, so on $s\in[-1,1]$ its range is $\left[\frac1e-2e,\ e-\frac2e\right]$ and $e-\frac2e\approx1.982<2$.
A close call: $1+\sqrt3\approx2.7321$ versus $e\approx2.7183$ - compare numerically, do not assume.
General check: an equation $F(\sin x)=k$ has solutions iff $k$ lies in the range of $F$ on $[-1,1]$.

questions.question: The number of solutions of the equation $4\sin^2x-4\cos^3x+9-4\cos x=0;\ x\in[-2\pi,2\pi]$ is :
questions.key_idea: Write $4\sin^2x=4-4\cos^2x$; the equation becomes $4\cos^3x+4\cos^2x+4\cos x=13$ while the left side is at most $12$.
solution: Since $\cos x\le1$, each term is at most its value at $\cos x=1$, so LHS $\le4+4+4=12$ (the PDF writes the LHS $\le12$).
$12<13$, so the equation has no solution: the number of solutions is $0$, option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Let $c=\cos x\in[-1,1]$ and study $g(c)=4c^3+4c^2+4c$: $g'(c)>0$ always, so $g$ is increasing and $g(c)\le g(1)=12<13$.
solution: Thus $g$ is strictly increasing on $[-1,1]$ and its range is $[g(-1),g(1)]=[-4,12]$.
$13\notin[-4,12]$, so there is no real $x$: $0$ solutions, option (A). Same answer.

useful_results: Convert to one function ($\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x$) and compare the equation with the range of that expression on $[-1,1]$.
The range of $g(c)=4c^3+4c^2+4c$ on $[-1,1]$ is $[-4,12]$ because $g'>0$; the constant $13$ lies outside.
Equality in a bound requires every term to be at its maximum together: here that would be $\cos x=1$, giving $12\ne13$.
The interval $[-2\pi,2\pi]$ plays no role once the equation has no solution for any $x$.

concepts: Trigonometric equations: range of a parameter
questions.question: Let the set of all $a\in R$ such that the equation $\cos2x+a\sin x=2a-7$ has a solution be $[p,q]$ and $r=\tan9^\circ-\tan27^\circ-\frac1{\cot63^\circ}+\tan81^\circ$, then $pqr$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Factor to $(\sin x-2)\left(a-2(\sin x+2)\right)=0$, so $a=2(\sin x+2)\in[2,6]$; and $\tan\theta+\cot\theta=\frac2{\sin2\theta}$ evaluates $r$.
solution: $\cos2x+a\sin x=2a-7\Rightarrow1-2\sin^2x+a\sin x-2a+7=0$, i.e. $a(\sin x-2)=2(\sin^2x-4)=2(\sin x-2)(\sin x+2)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Part 1: treat the equation as a quadratic in $\sin x$ whose roots are $2$ and $\frac{a-4}2$. Part 2: $\sin54^\circ-\sin18^\circ=2\cos36^\circ\sin18^\circ$ gives $r$ with no exact surds.
solution: $2s^2-as+2a-8=0$ with $s=\sin x$; its roots multiply to $a-4$ and one root is $s=2$ (substitute: $8-2a+2a-8=0$).
So the other root is $s=\frac{a-4}2$, and a solution exists iff $\left|\frac{a-4}2\right|\le1$, i.e. $a\in[2,6]$: $p=2,q=6$.

useful_results: $\tan\theta+\cot\theta=\frac2{\sin2\theta}$; $\tan(90^\circ-\theta)=\cot\theta$, so $\tan81^\circ=\cot9^\circ$ and $\tan63^\circ=\cot27^\circ$.
Classic: $\tan9^\circ-\tan27^\circ-\tan63^\circ+\tan81^\circ=4$ (numerically $3.99999\ldots$ checked).
$\sin18^\circ=\frac{\sqrt5-1}4$, $\cos36^\circ=\sin54^\circ=\frac{\sqrt5+1}4$, and $\sin54^\circ-\sin18^\circ=\frac12$.
If the equation is linear in the parameter ($a$), solve $a=g(\sin x)$ and take the range of $g$, after excluding any factor such as $\sin x-2$ that cannot vanish.

questions.question: Suppose $\theta\in\left[0,\frac\pi4\right]$ is a solutions of $4\cos\theta-3\sin\theta=1$. Then $\cos\theta$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Isolate $4\cos\theta-1=3\sin\theta$ and square to get a quadratic in $\cos\theta$; the interval $\left[0,\frac\pi4\right]$ picks the root.

alternate_solutions.idea: Auxiliary angle: $4\cos\theta-3\sin\theta=5\cos(\theta+\varphi)$ with $\cos\varphi=\frac45$; then $\theta=\beta-\varphi$ with $\cos\beta=\frac15$ and use the subtraction formula.
solution: $\theta+\varphi=\beta$ gives $\theta=\beta-\varphi\approx1.3694-0.6435=0.7259\in\left[0,\frac\pi4\right]$ (the other branch $\theta+\varphi=-\beta$ gives a negative $\theta$).

useful_results: $a\cos\theta+b\sin\theta=R\cos(\theta-\varphi)$, $R=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, $\cos\varphi=\frac aR$, $\sin\varphi=\frac bR$; here $4\cos\theta-3\sin\theta=5\cos(\theta+\varphi)$ with $\varphi=\tan^{-1}\frac34$.
Squaring creates extraneous roots - test with the interval: $\cos\theta\ge\cos\frac\pi4\approx0.707$ rejects $\frac{4-6\sqrt6}{25}\approx-0.43$ and leaves $0.748$.
Existence check via the sign change: at $\theta=0$ the left side is $4>1$ and at $\frac\pi4$ it is $\frac1{\sqrt2}<1$, so a root lies in $\left[0,\frac\pi4\right]$.
Rationalise to match options: $\frac4{3\sqrt6-2}=\frac{4(3\sqrt6+2)}{50}$.

concepts: Quadratic equations: discriminant condition for real roots
questions.question: Let $S=\{\sin^22\theta:(\sin^4\theta+\cos^4\theta)x^2+(\sin2\theta)x+(\sin^6\theta+\cos^6\theta)=0$ has real roots$\}$. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the smallest and largest elements of the set $S$, respectively, then $3\left((\alpha-2)^2+(\beta-1)^2\right)$ equals ______.
questions.key_idea: With $t=\sin^22\theta$: $\sin^4\theta+\cos^4\theta=1-\frac t2$ and $\sin^6\theta+\cos^6\theta=1-\frac{3t}4$, so $D\ge0$ is a quadratic inequality in $t\in[0,1]$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $w=\cos2\theta$ instead of $t$: $\sin^4+\cos^4=\frac{1+w^2}2$, $\sin^6+\cos^6=\frac{1+3w^2}4$, and the condition becomes the bi-quadratic $3w^4+6w^2-1\le0$ in a variable that already lives in $[0,1]$ for $w^2$.
solution: $D\ge0\iff3w^4+6w^2-1\le0\iff w^2\le-1+\frac2{\sqrt3}\approx0.1547$ (the other root of the quadratic in $w^2$ is negative).

useful_results: $\sin^4\theta+\cos^4\theta=1-\frac12\sin^22\theta$ and $\sin^6\theta+\cos^6\theta=1-\frac34\sin^22\theta$; with $w=\cos2\theta$ they are $\frac{1+w^2}2$ and $\frac{1+3w^2}4$.
A set defined as $\{\sin^22\theta:\ \text{condition}\}$ is a set of values of $t=\sin^22\theta$: solve the condition for $t$, then intersect with $[0,1]$.
Forgetting $t\le1$ would give $\beta=2+\frac2{\sqrt3}\approx3.15$ - always intersect with the range of the underlying trigonometric quantity.
Check at $t=1$ ($\theta=\frac\pi4$): $\frac12x^2+x+\frac14=0$ has $D=1-\frac12>0$; at $t=0.8$ the quadratic has no real roots (verified).

concepts: Quadratic in $\sin x$ and graphical counting
questions.question: The number of solutions of $\sin^2x+(2+2x-x^2)\sin x-3(x-1)^2=0$, where $-\pi\le x\le\pi$, is ______.
questions.key_idea: Since $2+2x-x^2=3-(x-1)^2$, the expression factors as $(\sin x+3)\left(\sin x-(x-1)^2\right)$.
solution: Sketch $y=\sin x$ and the parabola $y=(x-1)^2$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$: they intersect at two points (one in $(0,1)$, one in $(1,2)$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Concavity: $g(x)=\sin x-(x-1)^2$ has $g''=-\sin x-2<0$, so $g$ has at most two zeros, and sign changes at $0,1,2$ show there are exactly two.
solution: As a quadratic in $s=\sin x$ with $p=(x-1)^2$: $s^2+(3-p)s-3p=0$ has discriminant $(3-p)^2+12p=(p+3)^2$, so $s=p$ or $s=-3$.
$s=-3$ is impossible, so the equation is $g(x)=\sin x-(x-1)^2=0$.
$g''(x)=-\sin x-2\le-1<0$, so $g$ is strictly concave on $[-\pi,\pi]$ and has at most two zeros.
$g(0)=-1<0$, $g(1)=\sin1>0$, $g(2)=\sin2-1<0$: by the intermediate value theorem there is a zero in $(0,1)$ and one in $(1,2)$.
So there are exactly $2$ solutions (numerically $x\approx0.386$ and $x\approx1.962$). Same answer.

useful_results: For a quadratic in $\sin x$ with $x$-dependent coefficients, test whether the discriminant is a perfect square: here $D=\left((x-1)^2+3\right)^2$, giving roots $\sin x=(x-1)^2$ and $\sin x=-3$.
Concave (or convex) $g$ on an interval has at most two zeros there - a rigorous replacement for 'the graphs meet twice'.
Bounds shrink the search: $\sin x=(x-1)^2$ needs $0\le(x-1)^2\le1$, so $x\in[0,2]$; negative $x$ are excluded at once.
Sign-change checks at a few points ($g(0)<0$, $g(1)>0$, $g(2)<0$) locate the roots: $x\approx0.386$ and $1.962$.
